title: The man who coined ‘agentic AI’ is betting it won’t take your job
excerpt: Andrew Ng helped give the AI industry its vocabulary, from “AI is the new electricity” to “agentic AI.” His new company bets against the phrase everyone else is using: that AI will take your job. Ng has founded LearnVector, an AI-native learning startup, and Coursera is backing it with $100m, first reported by Axios. The […]
content_html:
Andrew Ng helped give the AI industry its vocabulary, from “AI is the new electricity” to “agentic AI.” His new company bets against the phrase everyone else is using: that AI will take your job.

Ng has founded LearnVector, an AI-native learning startup, and Coursera is backing it with $100m, first reported by Axios. The plan is AI agents that act as personal tutors. They adapt to each learner and drill with them until the learner can prove they have mastered a skill.

The premise rejects the layoffs narrative outright. Amazon, Meta and Block have all pinned recent job cuts partly on AI. Ng thinks that framing is wrong.

“Conventional wisdom holds that AI will replace people, and I believe in the opposite,” Ng told Reuters. AI will make workers more productive and create fresh demand for skills, he argues, rather than a “job apocalypse.”

What the money buys

The $100m gives Coursera roughly a one-third stake in LearnVector. That implies a valuation of about $300m for a company with no product yet.

It is a meaningful bet. The sum is close to 13% of the $790m in cash Coursera held at the end of March. The first LearnVector courses are due in early 2027.

The target is white-collar workers and other adults, not schoolchildren or university students. Ng plans to sell to corporations, governments and higher education. The pitch is teaching people the skills that keep them useful as AI automates parts of their work.

The part worth reading twice

Ng is not an outside founder Coursera happened to back. He co-founded Coursera in 2012 and still chairs it. This is a deal between a company and its own leadership.

Coursera says it handled that properly. A special committee of independent directors reviewed the terms and approved the investment unanimously.

“We had an opportunity to invest at the formation of a brand new company from one of the world’s foremost experts on AI,” Coursera chief executive Greg Hart told Axios. “That was incredibly appealing.”

The structure is disclosed and the process holds up. It still deserves stating plainly. A $100m related-party investment is not an everyday line item.

Why not just a chatbot

The obvious question is what LearnVector does that a chatbot cannot. A student can already ask any assistant to explain a concept.

Hart’s answer is persistence and rigour. A one-shot answer, he argues, engages a learner less than a system built around a serious view of the skill being taught.

Whether that holds up is unknown, because the product does not exist yet. Ng told Reuters he is still working out course offerings, pricing and the interface. LearnVector also runs on foundation models from a variety of third parties. The differentiator, for now, is Coursera’s content and its data on how people learn, not the AI itself.

Into a sceptical market

The company launches into real doubt about AI in education. Teachers, students and parents are still working out how AI helps learning without fuelling cheating. School AI policies remain patchy.

Targeting adults rather than classrooms sidesteps the sharpest version of that fight. It lands instead in the reskilling debate, where the evidence is mixed. Some studies question whether AI is driving job cuts at all, and adoption often spreads wide without going deep.

The backdrop is a labour market already nervous about AI. Workers report being penalised for using AI honestly. Recruiters are pivoting to specialised AI roles as their own jobs shift. Layoffs keep arriving with AI cited as the reason.

Ng’s pitch is that this anxiety is the market. If AI keeps changing what work requires, someone has to teach the new skills, and he wants that to be a tutor rather than a search box. It is an optimistic reading of a moment many people are living as loss, and it echoes his message to graduates entering the AI economy. Andrew Ng gets until 2027 to show the tutor works.

content_html_zh:
吴恩达为人工智能行业提供了从“人工智能是新电力”到“代理人工智能”的词汇。 他的新公司反对其他人都在使用的一句话：人工智能将取代你的工作。

Axios 最先报道称，Ng 创立了 LearnVector，这是一家人工智能原生学习初创公司，Coursera 为其提供了 1 亿美元的支持。 该计划是充当私人导师的人工智能代理。 他们适应每个学习者并与他们一起练习，直到学习者能够证明他们已经掌握了一项技能。

这个前提完全拒绝了裁员的说法。 亚马逊、Meta 和 Block 都将最近的裁员部分归咎于人工智能。 吴认为这个框架是错误的。

“传统观点认为人工智能将取代人类，但我的看法恰恰相反，”吴恩达告诉路透社。 他认为，人工智能将提高工人的工作效率，并创造新的技能需求，而不是“工作末日”。

钱买什么

来自欧盟科技界的最新传言、我们明智的创始人鲍里斯的故事，以及一些值得怀疑的人工智能艺术。 每周都会免费发送到您的收件箱中。 立即注册！

这 1 亿美元让 Coursera 获得了 LearnVector 大约三分之一的股份。 这意味着一家尚未推出产品的公司的估值约为 3 亿美元。

这是一个有意义的赌注。 该金额接近 Coursera 3 月底持有的 7.9 亿美元现金的 13%。 第一批 LearnVector 课程将于 2027 年初到期。

目标是白领工人和其他成年人，而不是小学生或大学生。 吴恩达计划向企业、政府和高等教育机构出售产品。 该项目旨在向人们传授一些技能，让他们在人工智能实现部分工作自动化时保持有用。

值得读两遍的部分

Ng并不是Coursera碰巧回来的外部创始人。 他于 2012 年与他人共同创立了 Coursera，目前仍担任该公司的主席。 这是公司与其领导层之间的交易。

Coursera 表示它处理得很好。 独立董事特别委员会审查了条款并一致批准了这项投资。

Coursera 首席执行官格雷格·哈特 (Greg Hart) 告诉 Axios：“我们有机会投资由世界上最重要的人工智能专家之一组建的全新公司。” “这非常有吸引力。”

结构已公开，过程也成立。 还是值得说清楚的。 1 亿美元的关联方投资并不是日常项目。

为什么不只是一个聊天机器人

显而易见的问题是 LearnVector 能做什么而聊天机器人却不能。 学生已经可以要求任何助手解释一个概念。

哈特的答案是坚持和严谨。 他认为，一次性的答案比一个围绕所教授的技能的严肃观点构建的系统更能吸引学习者。

这是否成立尚不清楚，因为该产品尚不存在。 吴告诉路透社，他仍在制定课程设置、定价和界面。 LearnVector 还可以在来自各种第三方的基础模型上运行。 目前，差异化因素是 Coursera 的内容及其关于人们如何学习的数据，而不是人工智能本身。

进入一个持怀疑态度的市场

该公司对人工智能在教育领域的应用产生了真正的怀疑。 教师、学生和家长仍在研究人工智能如何帮助学习而不助长作弊。 学校人工智能政策仍然不完整。

针对成年人而不是教室，回避了这场斗争的最激烈版本。 相反，它陷入了关于重新培训技能的争论，其中的证据是混杂的。 一些研究质疑人工智能是否会导致裁员，而且人工智能的采用往往很广泛，但没有深入。

背景是劳动力市场已经对人工智能感到紧张。 工人们报告因诚实使用人工智能而受到惩罚。 随着自己工作的转变，招聘人员正在转向专门的人工智能角色。 裁员不断到来，人工智能被认为是原因。

吴恩达的说法是，这种焦虑就是市场。 如果人工智能不断改变工作要求，就必须有人教授新技能，他希望这个人成为导师而不是搜索框。 这是对许多人生活在失落中的时刻的乐观解读，也呼应了他向进入人工智能经济的毕业生传达的信息。 Andrew Ng 可以在 2027 年之前展示导师的作品。
